title: Riding home
hook: sixth picture: he rides the ox home, playing the flute

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth picture: the ox grows gentle through patient tending, until it follows without a rope. Your line: tamed.

Evening. A path through the fields. An ox walks slowly toward a village, and on its back sits a man who isn't holding the rope at all. He has a flute to his lips, playing a simple tune, the kind children sing. Sometimes he looks up at the clouds. The ox knows the way. Two pictures ago this same animal was dragging him toward the hills. In the sixth oxherding picture, there's nothing left to hold.
screen: `EVENING, A PATH THROUGH THE FIELDS.` → `NO HAND ON THE ROPE.` → `A FLUTE AND THE CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: First, the struggle is over. The preface says it plainly, in paraphrase: the struggle has ended, and gain and loss no longer grip him. The rope that went taut in the fourth picture has nothing left to do. What was effort has become ease. Second, the flute. He plays country songs, the preface says, the tunes of woodcutters and children. Nothing grand, nothing that needs an audience. In this teaching, practice that's gone deep doesn't look solemn. It looks relaxed, even a little playful. Third, he doesn't turn back. If someone calls to him, the preface says, he won't look back; if someone tugs at him, he won't stop. Ease isn't drifting. He's going home, and he isn't distracted from it. Fourth, home. Some Zen teachers read home as one's own original nature, the place the search set out from. He isn't traveling somewhere new; he's going back. His eyes are on the sky, because the path no longer needs watching. On an ordinary day, riding home can look like a practice you no longer have to force: a walk you take because you like it, a pause before meals that just happens. The verse ends, in paraphrase, by saying that whoever knows this melody needs no words.
screen: `THE STRUGGLE IS OVER.` · `A FLUTE, A COUNTRY SONG.` · `CALLED, HE DOESN'T TURN BACK.` · `GOING HOME, NOT SOMEWHERE NEW.` · then, large: `RIDING HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit however feels comfortable, and let the breath do what it's already doing, without steering it. If a sound arrives, let it be music; if a thought calls, you don't have to turn around. The ox knows the way, so fix nothing, and if a small smile shows up, let it stay.
Riding home. The sixth oxherding picture: the struggle over, the herdsman rides the ox home playing a flute, untroubled by gain and loss. Today's word.
Your line: riding home. No hand on the rope, and nowhere else to be. Enjoy the ride.

howItsDone: Zen teachers use the sixth oxherding picture to describe a stage where practice no longer feels like a fight, and the image of the herdsman playing the flute on the ox's back also appears in Zen painting.

chat.says: If practice gets easy and playful, doesn't that mean you've stopped trying?
options: Not in the sixth picture. Ease isn't drifting; he's going home and won't turn back.
Yes. Real practice should always feel solemn and hard, or it isn't working.
Yes. Once the ox is tame, the herdsman can stop going anywhere at all.
chat.meaning: The preface says the struggle is over, yet if someone calls or tugs, he won't look back. Ease, not drifting.
